title: Michigan Water Blues, Clarence Williams, Spencer Williams and Fats Waller
summary: Disputed authorship of Michigan Water Blues, comments on Fats Waller and Clarence Williams, and talk of Spencer Williams.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah, that's right, Charles. That's right. Well, he also, I talked to him, the last time I saw him was in New York, and he played the test pressings of those things just before they were issued. And he said that he didn't like the way he did Michigan Water. They insisted he do it that way, and he didn't want to do it that way. And I don't know what he had in mind.

Well, I'll say this about Michigan Water. Clarence Williams had published, claimed it, in 1923 about. Whereas, according to John Lewis, Tony was playing that thing years before that. And as far as the tune itself goes, the verse, I had heard it before that thing, considerably. And I think maybe they got the music of Clarence Williams, and had him follow that to a certain extent, because in a way he does follow, not too closely. But Clarence Williams doubtless picked it up from Tony or from somebody else around there. I never heard Tony play it, but I had heard it around the morning, Michigan Water Blues, after that. They used to say Michigan Water tastes like sherry wine, but the Mississippi Water tastes like turpentine. That was the first person I heard of him. He used to kid about or laugh about Clarence. He said, no, it was, I'll say his name. It was Fats Waller. He says, Fats, he says, he's interested to see a little bit of something here he likes, a little bit of something there he likes, a little bit of something somewhere else he likes. He puts them all together, you've got a Fats Waller piece. He said, but anyway, with Clarence Williams, he grabbed a hole. He grabbed a hole. He's a little bit of a hole.

Well, you know, I think that the much more talented composer than Clarence was the... Oh, that other one. Spencer. Spencer, yeah. Yeah, he was. Spencer was a beautiful thing. Well, Spencer was a pretty well-known piano player in New Orleans too, wasn't he?
I believe he was, and yet he never recorded.
